The study cohort is the 8,323 registry patients with known transport
mode. Five contrasts are prespecified, each with its own analysis
lock built by `create_contrast_locks()` on the shared cohort
(@tbl-cs-locks): the protocol's primary comparison C1 (Rescue.Co
against everyone else), C2 (Rescue.Co against non-ambulance arrival),
C3 (any ambulance against non-ambulance), C4 (Rescue.Co against other
ambulance, transfers included), and the PRIMARY cohort contrast
(Rescue.Co against other ambulance with inter-facility transfers and
prior-care patients excluded, the cohort the study's earlier
single-contrast demonstration analysed). The presented outcomes are
six-month mortality (`death_by_6mo`, the primary) and time to
ambulance arrival in minutes, the outcome whose extrapolated estimate
motivates the Introduction; severe disability (GOSE $\le$ 4, so the
rare category is the event) and the remaining registry outcomes run
through the same locks. Missing follow-up is handled by IPCW as the
primary missingness path with complete case as the sensitivity. The
outcome columns are physically absent from the design stage: the
locks carry masked placeholders, and the outcome store is joined only
at estimation.

```{r cs-locks-table, eval = !is.null(cs_locks), echo = FALSE}
#| label: tbl-cs-locks
lk <- cs_locks
names(lk) <- c("Contrast", "Comparison", "N", "Treated", "Control",
               "Design columns")
knitr::kable(lk, caption = "The five prespecified transport contrasts,
each under its own analysis lock on the shared known-transport cohort.
Design columns count the sanitised covariate set entering the
propensity model.")
```

Each lock declares the same estimand ladder before outcome access:
ATE as the primary, then trimmed ATE, ATT, and ATO as ordered
fallbacks, with a SEVERE support verdict as the switching trigger and
a matched ATT carried as a sensitivity analysis. Ninety design
columns survive the `sanitize_covariates()` near-zero-variance and
aliasing filters, covering demographics, injury place, mechanism and
intent, severity (GCS, ISS components), distance, payment, SES
proxies, the chronic-condition panel, and calendar time. The
propensity library is the `build_sl_library()` "rwe_wide" preset
(penalised logistic learners, PCA-reduced GLMs, and the marginal
mean; no tree learners, which can separate arms on wide indicator
designs), with $V = 10$ following @phillips2023sl. Five negative
controls are registered on every lock, tagged with their
@muntner2024staging confounding domains: urban household and
wood-or-charcoal cooking fuel (health-seeking behaviour, access to
care), and hypertension, insulin-treated diabetes, and HIV on ART
(confounding by indication, functional status). Care-process
indicators (vitals missingness, examination markers) are registered
for the collider check and excluded from the adjustment set.

## The design stage: support and estimand feasibility {#sec-casestudy-support}

@tbl-cs-support shows the support assessment per contrast, computed
by `assess_support()` on each lock's fitted propensity.

```{r cs-support-table, eval = !is.null(cs_sup), echo = FALSE}
#| label: tbl-cs-support
sp <- cs_sup[, c("contrast", "pct_outside_band", "max_iptw_weight",
                 "ess_treated", "ess_control", "c_statistic", "verdict")]
names(sp) <- c("Contrast", "% outside [0.05, 0.95]", "Max IPTW weight",
               "ESS treated", "ESS control", "c-statistic", "Verdict")
knitr::kable(sp, digits = c(NA, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, NA),
  caption = "Support assessment by contrast on the fitted propensity
score. The effective sample size (ESS) is the Kish approximation under
ATE weights. The verdict thresholds are the package defaults stated in
the locks.")
```

The protocol comparison C1 places
`r round(.sup("C1", "pct_outside_band"), 1)`% of the sample outside
the band with a maximum ATE weight of
`r round(.sup("C1", "max_iptw_weight"))`, and C2 is nearly as bad;
both are graded SEVERE, which is the declared ladder trigger. The
violation is not a thin tail. The tree search localises it to
interpretable regions: patients injured at home (1,386 patients, 1.4%
treated), other non-street injury places, and assault victims outside
those places (4.2% treated). These patients essentially never receive
Rescue.Co transport, so the counterfactual "everyone transported by
Rescue.Co" is unanswerable for them without extrapolation. C3 and C4
are graded FLAG, and the PRIMARY cohort contrast passes
(`r round(.sup("PRIMARY", "pct_outside_band"), 2)`% outside, maximum
weight `r round(.sup("PRIMARY", "max_iptw_weight"))`): restricting to
ambulance arrivals without transfers or prior care removes the
never-treated strata, at the cost of a narrower question.

The per-estimand feasibility table then reads each fitted propensity
per estimand. On C1 the ATE is infeasible, while the ATT bounds its
control weights at 5.0 (the largest treated propensity is 0.85), the
ATO bounds all weights at 1 by construction, and the trimmed ATE
retains 4,946 patients after removing 3,377, nearly all controls. The
removal profile makes the estimand change concrete: the removed
patients are far more often injured at home (40% versus 1% of the
retained, standardised difference 1.10) or in assaults (39% versus
10%), are younger, live farther away, and more often sought prior
care. A trimmed analysis of C1 is not about those patients, and the
design report says so in words rather than leaving the shift implicit
[@crump2009trimming].

```{r cs-support-fig, eval = file.exists(file.path(.ma, "fig_support_C1.png")), echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Mirrored propensity histograms for the protocol contrast C1 (left) and the PRIMARY cohort contrast (right). Treated propensities are plotted above the axis and controls below, with the [0.05, 0.95] band shaded. The C1 control mass piled against zero is the severe violation; the PRIMARY contrast shows the two arms sharing support.", out.width = "49%", fig.show = "hold"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(file.path(.ma, "fig_support_C1.png"),
                          file.path(.ma, "fig_support_PRIMARY.png")))
```

### The outcome-blind support map

`simulate_support()` ran 200 generate-treatment replicates per
contrast over the prespecified surface family (synthetic confounding
strength 0, 1, 2 along the separating direction, crossed with effect
modification off and on) and scored each estimand's estimator against
a bias tolerance of 0.01 at a coverage floor of 0.90. Two readings of
the resulting map matter, and they answer different questions.

On C1 the map corroborates the static verdict from an independent
direction: the ATE fails at the mildest surface (coverage 0.87 while
the bounded estimands sit at 0.95), before any synthetic confounding
is added, which is the signature of a support failure rather than of
the stress. The bounded estimands (ATT, ATO, matched ATT, and with
one marginal cell the trimmed ATE) hold through the moderate
surfaces and degrade only at the harshest rung. On the PRIMARY
contrast every estimand passes the mildest surface, and as the
synthetic confounding strengthens the unmatched estimands degrade
together (coverage 0.81 to 0.89 at the harshest rung) while the
matched ATT holds 0.93 to 0.96 throughout; degradation that arrives
only with the stress, and hits all weighting-based estimands alike,
reads as confounding-strength stress rather than as a positivity
problem, consistent with the PASS verdict. These two patterns are
the map's value: it separates "fails because the design lacks
support" (C1's ATE, failing at baseline) from "fails because the
stress is harsh" (the harshest rung everywhere). A summary rule that
requires a whole-grid pass conflates the two, and on these data
would keep only the matched ATT; the design reports therefore read
the map over the moderate-confounding region for the support
question and report the whole-grid result as a conservative bound,
a reading rule recorded in the design log before estimation.

### Generate-treatment versus sample-treatment on real data

```{r cs-designcmp, echo = FALSE}
.cmp_p <- file.path(.ma, "designcmp_C1.rds")
cs_cmp <- if (file.exists(.cmp_p)) readRDS(.cmp_p) else NULL
```

The C1 lock also reruns its support simulation under the legacy
sample-treatment design, holding everything else fixed, as a
real-data check of the @shaw2025plasmode argument
(@tbl-cs-designcmp). At the mild surface the two designs agree.
At the stressed surface the sample-treatment design, which carries
the observed 41% violation into every replicate, inflates the bias
of every bounded estimand by roughly half again (ATT 0.018 versus
0.013, ATO 0.016 versus 0.010) and collapses their coverage (ATT
0.69 versus 0.78, ATO 0.64 versus 0.79, matched ATT 0.63 versus
0.86), while the ATE's RMSE balloons more than fivefold (0.066
versus 0.012) as the replicated violation meets the stressed
surface. A support map built on the sample-treatment design would
therefore have declared every estimand infeasible on C1, not because
the design cannot support them but because the simulation
manufactured the failure it was asked to detect.

```{r cs-designcmp-table, eval = !is.null(cs_cmp), echo = FALSE}
#| label: tbl-cs-designcmp
cc <- cs_cmp[cs_cmp$confounding == 2 & cs_cmp$modification == 0,
             c("design", "estimand", "bias", "rmse", "coverage")]
cc$design <- ifelse(cc$design == "generate_treatment",
                    "generate", "sample")
names(cc) <- c("Design", "Estimand", "Bias", "RMSE", "Coverage")
knitr::kable(cc, digits = c(NA, NA, 4, 4, 2), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Plasmode design comparison on the C1 lock at the
stressed outcome surface (synthetic confounding strength 2), 200
replicates per design. The sample-treatment design reproduces the
observed positivity violation in every replicate and degrades every
estimand; the generate-treatment design lets the declared surface
family govern the stress.")
```

## Negative-control ladder and the collider check

The negative-control ladder fits all five registered controls,
unadjusted, on each nested cohort: the full contrast cohort, then
transfers excluded, then transfers and prior care excluded. On the
full C4 cohort the two socioeconomic controls fail decisively (urban
household +0.068, 95% CI 0.049 to 0.086; wood-or-charcoal fuel
$-$0.052, CI $-$0.074 to $-$0.029): ambulance transfer patients
differ socioeconomically from direct arrivals. Both turn null after
the transfer exclusion (urban household +0.001) and stay null after
the prior-care exclusion, and on the PRIMARY cohort every estimable
control is null. On C1 the urban-household control fails on the full
cohort (+0.013, CI 0.003 to 0.024) and has no restriction rung that
repairs it, which corroborates the support verdict from an
independent direction. Hypertension is null everywhere, and the two
rare chronic controls (insulin-treated diabetes, HIV on ART) are
labelled inestimable on every rung, following the
@conover2025diagnostics practice of reporting inestimability rather
than silently shrinking the panel. The reading is the study's second
methodological point: the pre-registered exclusions, not covariate
adjustment, removed the measurable confounding, and the ladder shows
which restriction did the work. A TMLE-adjusted variant of the same
ladder is reported in the supplement with a caveat: on the restricted
rungs it conditions on design columns that are near-copies of the
socioeconomic controls, so its restricted-rung rows are not
comparable to the unadjusted ladder.

The collider check regresses each care-process indicator on
treatment given severity. Vitals-recorded-within-an-hour and
blood-pressure-missingness are predicted by treatment on C3, C4, and
the PRIMARY contrast (standardised differences 0.11 to 0.34), which
is expected: transport mode changes the care process. The check
confirms these variables belong outside the adjustment set, where
the locks placed them; conditioning on them would open collider
paths through in-hospital care.

## Pre-outcome decision

`design_report()` assembles, per contrast, the support verdict, the
feasibility table, the support map, the negative-control ladder, and
the collider check, and closes with the recommendation the review
team reads. For the PRIMARY contrast the recommendation is to
proceed. For C1 and C2 it is to proceed with qualification: the
declared primary (ATE) is not supported, the ladder moves to the
trimmed ATE, then ATT, then ATO, and the switch is logged as a
design decision with the SEVERE verdict as its recorded trigger. For
C3 and C4 the recommendation is to proceed with the FLAG caveat
attached. Every recommendation was fixed, and the design log
exported, before the outcome store was joined.

## Candidate selection and the DQ stress test {#sec-casestudy-dq}

Candidate selection and the data-quality stress test were run on the
PRIMARY cohort's earlier single-contrast lock (functional outcome, four
TMLE candidates varying the propensity library and truncation:
`glm_t01`, `glmnet_t01`, `ensemble_t01`, `ensemble_t05`), and we report
them from that run; the multi-arm rebuild reuses the locked candidate.
The Stage 2b feasibility plasmode metrics on the locked DGP are:

| Candidate       | Bias     | RMSE   | Coverage |
|-----------------|---------:|-------:|---------:|
| `glm_t01`       | +0.00001 | 0.0134 |     0.92 |
| `ensemble_t05`  | +0.00076 | 0.0135 |     0.92 |
| `glmnet_t01`    | +0.00019 | 0.0135 |     0.92 |
| `ensemble_t01`  | +0.00082 | 0.0136 |     0.92 |

: Stage 2b feasibility plasmode metrics (rescueCo lock, 50 replicates
per candidate, additive risk-difference effect of 0.05). On the
clean-data baseline the four candidates are nearly tied (RMSE within
0.0002), so the `min_rmse` rule would pick `glm_t01`; under the
five-threat DQ sweep they separate, and the minimax rule picks
`ensemble_t05` instead.

All four candidates pass the prespecified decision targets
(`max_abs_bias = 0.01`, `min_coverage = 0.90`) on the clean-data
baseline, where their performance is nearly indistinguishable because
the propensity scores stay well inside the [0.01, 0.99] bounds
(range 0.21--0.81). Under the prespecified five-threat DQ sweep, the
worst-case RMSE ratio relative to baseline is 1.82 for `glm_t01`,
1.73 for `glmnet_t01`, 1.53 for `ensemble_t01`, and 1.27 for
`ensemble_t05`; the largest contributor for each candidate is the
near-positivity threat at slope $\times 4$. The minimax rule therefore
locks `ensemble_t05` (the heaviest truncation), while a baseline-only
rule would have locked `glm_t01` (the lowest baseline RMSE, but also
the most fragile candidate under stress). This makes the case study a
real-data instance of the divergence reported in @sec-divergence on a
constructed grid.

All four candidates passed the prespecified operating targets on the
well-overlapped PRIMARY cohort, where their baseline performance is
nearly indistinguishable. The Stage 2c DQ stress test sweeps the
prespecified five-threat grid (near-positivity, covariate missingness
under MCAR/MAR/MNAR, treatment and outcome misclassification, and
unmeasured confounding) over the candidate grid, and the minimax rule
locks `ensemble_t05` as the primary specification. This is itself a
divergence: the `min_rmse` rule would pick `glm_t01` (the lowest
baseline RMSE, 0.0134), but under the stress sweep `glm_t01` has the
highest worst-case RMSE ratio (1.82, driven by the near-positivity
threat), while `ensemble_t05` (which uses heavier truncation and a
small ensemble library) has the lowest (1.27). The case study
therefore reproduces, on a real-data lock, the same mechanism that the
constructed divergence study in @sec-divergence demonstrates: a
candidate selected for clean-data efficiency is the most exposed under
the prespecified threat sweep, and the minimax rule reroutes the
selection toward a more robust specification. The reported result uses a
50-replicate run (`rescueCo/scripts/rescueco_dq_full.R`, see
@sec-reproducibility), an illustration below the 200-replicate bar we
adopt for inferential interpretation, consistent with the case study
being a workflow demonstration rather than confirmatory evidence; a
200-replicate confirmation is the analyst's next step for a
submission-grade analysis. The 3-replicate configuration bundled with
the staged pipeline is a continuous-integration smoke test and is not
used for inference.

## Effect estimates

Estimation runs only after the design reports above are fixed.
`run_estimand_ladder()` executes per lock and outcome: the declared
primary (ATE) where the trigger was not met, and the feasible
fallbacks (trimmed ATE, ATT, ATO, with the matched ATT as
sensitivity) where it was. Each row carries its estimand label, the
lock's support verdict, and the implausibility flags, and the design
log records the C1 and C2 switches with the SEVERE verdict as their
trigger. @tbl-cs-ladder shows the six-month mortality rows.

```{r cs-ladder-table, echo = FALSE}
#| label: tbl-cs-ladder
.lad_p <- file.path(.ma, "ladder_estimates.csv")
if (file.exists(.lad_p)) {
  lad <- read.csv(.lad_p, check.names = FALSE)
  keep <- intersect(c("contrast", "outcome", "estimand", "n", "estimate",
                      "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "implausible"), names(lad))
  ld <- lad[grepl("death", lad$outcome), keep]
  if ("implausible" %in% names(ld))
    ld$implausible <- ifelse(is.na(ld$implausible), "",
                             ifelse(ld$implausible, "flagged", ""))
  names(ld) <- sub("^ci_lower$", "95% CI lower", names(ld))
  names(ld) <- sub("^ci_upper$", "95% CI upper", names(ld))
  knitr::kable(ld, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "Estimand-ladder estimates for six-month mortality
(risk differences), one row per contrast and feasible estimand,
produced by run_estimand_ladder() on the locked designs. Rows for the
severe-overlap contrasts C1 and C2 carry no ATE row; the ladder
switch is logged in the design log.")
} else {
  cat("Ladder estimates are generated by",
      "`rescueCo/scripts/13_multiarm_estimation.R`;",
      "the table renders once `ladder_estimates.csv` is present.")
}
```

Two readings of this table belong to the workflow rather than to the
substantive question. First, no C1 or C2 row answers the protocol's
original question: those contrasts report the trimmed, treated
population and overlap-weighted effects, each labelled with the
population it is about, because the design stage established that the
ATE is not estimable there. What a conventional pipeline would have
reported for C1, an IPTW or TMLE ATE under weights reaching
`r round(.sup("C1", "max_iptw_weight"))`, is exactly the kind of
estimate the Introduction's motivating failure warns about, and the
same ladder run re-analyses that failure's own outcome: time to
arrival, where an earlier full-cohort analysis produced +14,637
minutes against a crude difference of seven hours in the other
direction, is estimated here only through bounded-weight estimands,
with the implausibility guard comparing every row against the bounds
the raw arm summaries impose. Second,
the estimates that are reported agree with the parallel unblinded main
analysis of the same registry where the two pipelines are comparable;
the matched ATT on the functional dichotomy differs from the main
pipeline's estimate by well under a quarter of a standard error, and
the reconciliation table released with the case study tracks every
(contrast, outcome, estimand, estimator) pair across the two
pipelines. Per-row E-values [@vanderWeele2017evalue] via
`compute_evalue()` and outcome-missingness delta sensitivity via
`run_delta_sensitivity()` accompany the primary rows in the released
artifacts. The healthcare-worker strike period remains an unmodelled
threat that the prespecified threat families do not cover, and we
carry it as a limitation rather than a quantified scenario.

## What the case study tells us about the workflow

### Prespecification, the design log, and an honest failure

The design log captured every prespecified analytic choice (the
contrast definitions, the exclusions, the ladder declarations, the
truncation and threshold settings) with timestamps, and the lock
fingerprints reconciled on every reload. The most instructive record,
though, is a failure from the study's earlier single-contrast run.
That run's primary outcome was the *good*-outcome dichotomy of GOSE,
with prevalence 0.92, so the rare category carried too few events;
the cohort-adequacy checkpoint recorded STOP, and the pipeline
proceeded anyway through an unlogged override, a `tryCatch` around
the authorisation check with nothing recorded between the STOP and
the estimate. The September reconciliation against the parallel
unblinded analysis surfaced this precisely because the audit trail
had preserved both records: the STOP and the estimate, with no
rationale between them. The rebuild fixed the design rather than the
log: the outcome set was aligned to the main analysis (mortality as
primary, severe disability as the functional dichotomy, so the rare
category is the event), and overrides now require a logged reason,
so the record can no longer show STOP followed silently by
estimation. We report this candidly because it is the working theory
of the framework in miniature: the value of the record is that it
makes such gaps findable, including gaps in the workflow's own
conduct.

### Outcome-blind plasmode

Stage 2b feasibility coverage of 0.94 with bias below 0.001 across
50 replicates is the kind of design validation a reviewer would
want, and the 200-replicate support maps of @sec-casestudy-support
extend the same device to the estimability question. Stage 2c then
runs the full DQ stress test (`run_plasmode_dq_stress()`) over the
prespecified threat sweep and produces a structural pass on each
scenario at 50 replicates per threat-severity cell (an illustration
below the 200-replicate inferential bar; see @sec-reproducibility for
the entry point). The five threats encoded by
`run_plasmode_dq_stress()` (covariate missingness under
MCAR/MAR/MNAR, exposure misclassification, outcome misclassification,
latent $U$, and near-positivity) still do not cover one design
challenge that mattered in the rescueCo study, the strike-window
confounder, which motivates the time-window extension in
@sec-future.

### Synthetic-outcome fidelity

```{r casestudy-fidelity}
.fid_path <- "../rescueCo/results/plasmode_fidelity.csv"
if (file.exists(.fid_path)) {
  fv <- stats::setNames(read.csv(.fid_path)$value, read.csv(.fid_path)$metric)
} else {
  fv <- stats::setNames(rep(NA_real_, 5),
    c("n_complete_case", "real_prevalence", "Q0_auc_insample",
      "Q0_auc_cv", "calibration_max_abs_dev_cv"))
}
```

The plasmode resamples the empirical covariate structure of the
rescueCo cohort, redraws treatment from the fitted propensity
(@sec-support-map), and generates synthetic outcomes from a
covariate-only model $Q_0(W) = E[Y \mid W]$, so the synthetic covariate
marginals match the observed ones by construction. Because a
logistic $Q_0$ with an intercept forces the fitted mean to equal the observed
mean, a marginal prevalence match is automatic and is not by itself evidence of
fidelity, so we assess $Q_0$ out of sample instead. Fitting $Q_0(W)$ on the
earlier run's complete-case functional-outcome cohort
($n = `r fv[["n_complete_case"]]`$, outcome prevalence
`r round(fv[["real_prevalence"]], 3)`) and evaluating it by ten-fold
cross-validation, the covariate-only outcome model discriminates the observed
outcome with a cross-validated AUC of `r round(fv[["Q0_auc_cv"]], 2)` (the
in-sample AUC of `r round(fv[["Q0_auc_insample"]], 2)` is optimistic by
resubstitution), and its out-of-sample calibration has a maximum absolute
predicted-minus-observed deviation across risk deciles of
`r round(fv[["calibration_max_abs_dev_cv"]], 3)`. This establishes that the
plasmode preserves the covariate structure and a moderately discriminating,
reasonably calibrated marginal outcome model, not that it reproduces the joint
treatment-outcome law. The synthetic outcome carries a fixed risk difference
and no effect modification, and the fidelity of that joint structure to the
realised process cannot be checked before the outcome is unblinded, so the
diagnostic is a necessary rather than a sufficient fidelity check, consistent
with the limitation in @sec-discussion.

### Estimator functions and real-data robustness

Applying cleanTMLE 0.1.0 to the original rescueCo lock surfaced more
than a dozen distinct issues, six of them blocking, which the 0.1.x
releases addressed: `run_plasmode_dq_stress()` failed outright on a
lock with NA in the outcome (now guarded), the step-by-step TMLE
functions refused to fit on NA outcomes (now subset to complete cases
with an MCAR warning), the SuperLearner propensity fit crashed on
stale parallel backends (now sequential by default), and failed
negative-control fits were dropped silently (now recorded). The
multi-arm rebuild then drove the 0.2.0 redesign in the other
direction: the support assessment, the per-estimand feasibility
reading, the estimand ladder, and the generate-treatment plasmode all
exist because this study needed them, and the same rebuild
consolidated the exported surface from 149 functions to 54 after the
governance layer grew faster than its evidential value. We document
both directions candidly because the working theory of the framework
is that the prespecification record should make problems visible,
including problems with the package itself, rather than absorb them
into a hand-edited final table.

The full release notes are in `cleanTMLE/NEWS.md`, and the case
study's `results/multiarm/` directory contains the CSV artifacts
behind every table in this section, together with the reconciliation
table against the parallel unblinded analysis.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## What cleanTMLE contributes operationally

The novelty in this paper is not causal identification. The roadmap and
target-trial literature [@dang2023roadmap; @petersen2014roadmap;
@hernan2016targettrial] already provides that frame, and the package operates
inside its estimation and pre-outcome diagnostics steps. The novelty is that
two questions usually settled informally become explicit, prespecified
outputs of the blind phase. The first is estimability: the support
assessment, the per-estimand feasibility reading, the outcome-blind support
map, and the estimand ladder together answer "is this comparison estimable,
and with which estimand" before the outcome is examined, and convert any
estimand switch into a logged design decision. The second is robustness: the
DQ stress test adds a candidate-specific pre-outcome screen on top of the
standard plasmode loop. Around both, the analysis-lock object and the design
log make the prespecification a reproducible record, supporting transparent
reconstruction of paper-only prespecification checklists [@gruber2022sap;
@cashin2024target] by an external reviewer.

The contribution is operational, and a useful test is to ask what evidence the
package can and cannot produce. cleanTMLE can document that the analyst
prespecified the estimand ladder, the candidate estimators, the decision
thresholds, and the severity ranges; that the support and feasibility
verdicts, and any estimand switch, were fixed before unblinding; that the
locked candidate was the one that ran on the real outcome; and that a
fingerprinted record captures the sequence. cleanTMLE
cannot demonstrate that the data source is fit for the regulatory question,
that the exposure or outcome phenotypes have been validated, that the target
population is the regulatory decision population, or that the
unmeasured-confounder bound is defensible. Nor can the support machinery see
past the measured covariates: a propensity model that misses the separating
covariate will not warn, which is why the negative-control ladder and the
stratum checks run beside the global statistics. Those remain study-level
activities, anchored in target-trial protocols [@hernan2016targettrial;
@cashin2024target], source-specific guidance [@fda2024considerations;
@fda2024ehrclaims; @fda2021registries; @ema2024guide; @ema2026rwd], and
post-outcome sensitivity analyses [@vanderWeele2017evalue; @lash2014qba;
@diaz2013sensitivity].

## How the workflow aligns with regulatory expectations

For high-stakes regulatory or confirmatory RWE, cleanTMLE is best
used as one layer in a broader governed workflow. The lock and audit machinery track the
prespecification and traceability that FDA RWE program guidance,
EMA RWD guidance, and the NICE RWE framework expect [@fda2018rwe;
@fda2024considerations; @fda2024noninterventional; @ema2024guide;
@nice2022rwe] and match the data-quality dimensions
in the EMA RWD framework [@ema2026rwd] and ICH M14 (March 2026)
[@ich2024m14], as summarised in @tbl-reg-align. As stated in the abstract, the
software layer sits inside, rather than substitutes for, the
personnel-based governance this guidance requires: documented source
assessment, role-based access controls, and structured protocol records.

## Comparison with adjacent tools

@tbl-baselines places cleanTMLE against the nearest alternatives, to make
explicit which capabilities are shared and which are specific to the
package. The combination that distinguishes cleanTMLE is the
design-stage estimability answer (support assessment, per-estimand
feasibility, the support map, and the estimand ladder), the
outcome-blind plasmode candidate selection with the DQ stress test on
the same decision scale, and the prespecification record (lock and
design log), bound to a doubly robust estimator layer that reproduces a
mature cumulative-risk package (@sec-casestudy, and the side-by-side
ACTG 320 reproduction in the companion repository).

```{r baselines-table}
#| label: tbl-baselines
baselines <- data.frame(
  Capability = c(
    "Doubly robust TMLE",
    "Cumulative-risk / competing risks",
    "Time-varying treatment",
    "Graded support assessment + per-estimand feasibility",
    "Pre-registered estimand ladder with logged switching",
    "Outcome-blind plasmode candidate selection",
    "Data-quality stress test (shared decision scale)",
    "Prespecification lock + design log",
    "Fit-for-purpose to estimator-selection bridge"),
  `cleanTMLE` = c("Yes", "Yes (grammar verbs; ladder on roadmap)",
                  "No (compose with lmtp)", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes",
                  "Yes", "Yes"),
  `causalRisk` = c("AIPW", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No",
                   "No"),
  `tmle / survtmle / lmtp` = c("Yes", "survtmle / lmtp", "lmtp",
                               "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No"),
  `STaRT-RWE / HARPER + git/renv` = c("No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No",
                                      "No",
                                      "Paper template; not machine-checked",
                                      "No"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(baselines,
  caption = "cleanTMLE against adjacent tools. The estimator layer overlaps with established packages; the design-stage estimability answer, the outcome-blind selection, the DQ stress test, and the machine-checkable prespecification record are the distinguishing combination.")
```

The contrast with the E-value is treated once in @sec-evalue, where the
post-hoc E-value and the pre-hoc, candidate-specific DQ stress test are shown
to answer different questions and to be worth reporting together.

Quantitative bias analysis [@lash2014qba] adjusts the final
estimate for postulated biases. Like the E-value, QBA is an
unblinding-stage tool. The DQ stress test does not adjust the
estimate; it asks whether the estimator continues to meet the
prespecified performance criteria when the biases are present. We
therefore recommend QBA at the analysis stage and the DQ stress
test at the prespecification stage.

The targeted-learning causal-gap sensitivity analysis
[@diaz2013sensitivity] characterises the change in $\Psi$ as the
unmeasured-confounder bound varies. Causal-gap is unblinding-stage
and characterises one threat (unmeasured confounding) in a TL-
specific way. The DQ stress test is broader (it covers five
threats) but cruder (it does not adjust the estimate). Both are
useful and complementary.

Negative-control outcomes [@lipsitch2010negative] test for
residual confounding in the realised data. Because they use real
data, they are at-outcome rather than pre-outcome. The DQ stress
test cannot detect residual confounding; the NCO check cannot
detect covariate missingness or exposure misclassification. They
target different threats. @muntner2024staging recommend selecting
NCOs across four domains (confounding by indication, functional
status, health-seeking behaviour, and access to healthcare) and
@levintow2023nco give pragmatic guidance for choosing them; the
cleanTMLE workflow records each declared NCO in the lock so the
chosen domains are part of the audit trail.

@kent2026fiord reports a worked applied use of the staging
framework for a comparative-effectiveness study of evolocumab
versus non-treatment for major adverse cardiovascular events in
the Komodo Healthcare Map: negative-control outcomes flagged
residual bias in the health-seeking-behaviour domain, the review
team allowed the study to proceed conditional on a pre-specified
E-value quantitative-bias-analysis plan, and the final risk
difference at four years was reported as roughly $-4\%$. The
example illustrates both the staged decision rule and the role of
negative-control domains in practice.

## Limitations of plasmode data-quality stress testing {#sec-limitations}

A plasmode data-quality stress test is only as informative as the
synthetic outcome model and degradation mechanisms used to
generate it. Passing the pre-outcome decision rule does not
establish identification, remove unmeasured confounding, validate
the data source, or demonstrate that the target population matches
the regulatory decision population. It shows only that, under the
prespecified outcome-generating mechanism and degradation ranges,
a candidate estimator maintained acceptable finite-sample
performance according to the chosen criteria. Severity ranges
should therefore be justified from external validation studies,
data profiling, subject-matter knowledge, expert elicitation, or
formal sensitivity-analysis bounds. When such evidence is weak,
the stress test should be interpreted as exploratory rather than
confirmatory.

The DQ stress test also depends on the same parametric
synthetic-outcome model used by the baseline plasmode. If that
model misrepresents the joint covariate-treatment-outcome
distribution (for example by omitting effect modification or
mis-specifying functional form), the simulated bias and coverage
under stressed scenarios may be optimistic or pessimistic in ways
that no amount of replication can correct.

## Other limitations

The current implementation has additional limitations the
analyst should keep in mind, grouped into the candidate-selection
rule, model assumptions, computational cost, and estimand scope.

### Candidate-selection rule (FIORD alignment)

The FIORD outcome-blind simulation guidance [@nance2026fiord] separates
candidate selection into two tasks: first screen point estimators by
oracle coverage (a CI built from the Monte Carlo empirical SE) and pick
the lowest-variance survivor, then select the variance method on the
locked point estimator using nominal CI coverage. cleanTMLE implements
both stages. Stage one is `select_tmle_candidate(rule = "fiord_two_stage")`,
which screens candidates to those within `fiord_coverage_tol` of nominal
oracle coverage and locks in the lowest-SE survivor (the default
`rule = "min_rmse"`, optionally `"min_max_rmse"` over the DQ stress
scenarios, remains available as a single-step alternative). Stage two is
`select_variance_method()`, which, with the point estimator fixed,
compares variance methods by their oracle coverage on synthetic data and
returns the one closest to nominal; `bootstrap_rd_variance()` supplies a
native nonparametric bootstrap standard error and percentile interval for
the marginal risk difference under TMLE or stabilised IPTW. The bootstrap
is one option when the influence-function variance is suspect. For
stabilised IPTW the influence-function variance treats the propensity score
as known (@robins1992rotnitzky), and resampling does not remove that
conservatism, so the bootstrap interval is reported alongside the
influence-function interval and the better-calibrated one is chosen on
oracle coverage. For a matched cohort the standard nonparametric bootstrap
is not consistent (@abadie2008bootstrap), and the full-pipeline re-matching
variant is reported as an empirical correction. The remaining limitation is
practical. The variance-method stage is exposed as a separate call and is
not folded into a single `run_*` wrapper, and the bootstrap multiplies
computation, so analysts reserve it for the estimators where the IF variance
is known to misbehave.

### Model assumptions

The covariate-missingness scenario degrades $W$ under MCAR, MAR, and
MNAR masks, so the stress test can probe missingness that depends on
observed covariates (MAR) or on the masked value itself (MNAR). The
only missing-data handling exercised, however, is median imputation:
the degraded covariate is filled with its column median before each
candidate is refit. A principled alternative is
inverse-probability-of-missingness weighting or multiple imputation,
which under MAR recovers valid inference where median imputation does
not; a native cleanTMLE implementation of that path is future work.

The plasmode DGP itself is parametric. The outcome is generated
from a logistic regression of $Y$ on $W$ fitted to the lock data,
and the synthetic effect is constant on the risk-difference scale
($p_1^{\text{sim}} = p_0^{\text{sim}} + \Delta$). Effect
modification, time-varying treatment, and competing risks would
need a richer DGP. The package architecture permits these
extensions; the simulation reported here does not exercise them.
cleanTMLE 0.2.1 adds a `q0_library` argument to
`run_plasmode_feasibility()` so the analyst can fit Q0 with a
SuperLearner library rather than the default logistic GLM; this
relaxes the bias of candidate selection toward linear-in-logit
learners when the underlying outcome surface is nonlinear. A
companion pilot simulation (`plasmode_selection_paper/`) provides
the empirical motivation: at n = 500, a logistic-GLM Q0 yields
no detectable separation between fixed-library and plasmode-
selected TMLE workflows because both inherit the same linearity
bias.

The plausible degradation ranges have to come from external
evidence. The software cannot decide whether 5 % or 20 %
covariate missingness is realistic for a given data source; the
analyst has to cite a profiling or validation study. SPIFD2 makes
the same demand qualitatively, and the DQ stress test inherits it.

### PS candidate grid and learner stability

The DQ stress test generates synthetic outcomes under degraded
covariate, treatment, and confounder distributions, and then re-fits
every candidate PS model on each synthetic dataset. The synthetic
designs for Scenario B (marginal overlap, PS range 0.037--0.990)
produced numerical instability in regularised learners: SL.glmnet
ran away on computation with no convergence signal, inflating wall
time by more than an order of magnitude relative to GLM. The
simulation in @sec-simulation therefore uses a three-candidate GLM PS
grid ($t \in \{0.001, 0.025, 0.20\}$) for the DQ stress test; SL.glmnet is
retained in the SuperLearner library for the cross-fitted TMLE
nuisance fits, where it operates on the full (undegraded)
observed-data sample. In practice, the GLM and regularised-learner
PS produce near-identical plasmode metrics on the simple logistic DGP
used here, so the omission does not change the candidate-selection
outcome. Analysts with more complex DGPs or learner libraries that
include tree-based or spline models should profile DQ-stress runtime
on a small representative run before committing to a full grid.

### Computational cost

Each scenario $\times$ severity cell adds a full set of plasmode
replicates. With the configuration of @sec-simulation (30 plasmode
replicates per cell, 19 degraded severity cells, and three PS
candidates) the stress test fits about 1,700 candidate TMLE models
per Monte Carlo scenario, or roughly 6,800 across the four scenarios,
alongside the undegraded baseline plasmode. Each fit uses a
GLM-nuisance TMLE, so a full per-scenario run, including the
200-replicate main Monte Carlo, completed in about twelve minutes on
a current multi-core workstation in our runs, and the four-scenario
study fits inside a conventional statistical-analysis-plan timeline.
Larger candidate grids or higher replicate counts scale linearly;
parallelising over severity cells is the most direct route for
interactive use.

### Estimand scope

The running estimands in this paper are marginal risk contrasts for a
binary point exposure: the ATE and its trimmed version, the ATT, and
the overlap-weighted ATO, all on the risk-difference scale, with
multi-arm exposures handled as prespecified pairwise contrasts under
shared-cohort locks. The companion cumulative-risk grammar covers
time-to-event risks with censoring and competing risks, but the
staged support-and-ladder machinery has not yet been extended to
those estimands. Counterfactual hazard ratios, longitudinal
treatments, and cumulative-count estimands sit outside the current
scope; analysts who need them have `survtmle`
[@survtmlepackage2018] and `lmtp` [@lmtppackage2021] as alternative
implementations, and can feed their output through the same lock
records.

## Future extensions {#sec-future}

The most consequential extensions, in priority order, are:

1. **Single-call FIORD alignment.** Both FIORD stages are now
   implemented (`select_tmle_candidate(rule = "fiord_two_stage")` for the
   point estimator, and `select_variance_method()` with
   `bootstrap_rd_variance()` for the variance method; see also
   @mertens2024danish). Folding the variance stage into a single `run_*`
   wrapper and caching the bootstrap would make full FIORD alignment the
   one-call default rather than two explicit steps.
2. **Operating-characteristic validation of the variance selector** at
   scale, paired with the gate validation in @sec-gate-oc, so the
   variance-method choice is itself shown to recover nominal coverage
   across a range of data-generating processes.
3. **Unmeasured-confounding severity gradient:** vary the strength
   of the latent-U scenario across a prespecified grid rather than
   running a single strong-U setting, so the DQ stress test
   produces an E-value-style sensitivity curve as a by-product.
4. **Pre-protocol stress-test mode:** allow the plasmode and DQ
   stress test to run on user-specified covariate distributions
   and treatment-mechanism strength (no real data required) so
   that investigators can decide which dataset to use before any
   data-use agreement is signed.
5. **DGP-spectrum argument** for the plasmode generator: structural-
   equation (`simcausal`-style), hybrid (current default), and
   parametric-bootstrap modes, with synthetic-data fidelity metrics
   (Hellinger / Wasserstein, or covariate SMDs between real and
   synthetic samples) so the analyst can judge whether the DGP is
   faithful enough to base candidate selection on.
6. **Matched-cohort vs full-cohort plasmode diagnostic:** under a
   known synthetic truth, compare the two estimators side by side
   to diagnose whether observed real-data gaps are sampling noise
   or positivity-driven.
7. **Richer synthetic-outcome models:** effect modification, time-
   varying treatment, and competing risks (the current DGP is a
   logistic regression with a constant additive effect on the
   risk-difference scale).
8. **MAR / MNAR missingness handling:** the data-quality stress test
   now degrades covariates under MAR and MNAR, but the only handling it
   exercises is median imputation; a native inverse-probability-of-
   missingness or multiple-imputation path that does not require a
   structural missingness model remains future work.
9. **Survival and competing-risk estimands:** wrapping `survtmle`
   [@survtmlepackage2018] and `lmtp` [@lmtppackage2021] (and
   `ltmle` for the longitudinal FIORD setting) inside the lock
   and audit machinery so that hazard-ratio and cumulative-
   incidence estimands inherit the same governance.
10. **Transportability and decision-population shift:** the
    plasmode framework can in principle simulate covariate-
    distribution shift between the analytic cohort and the target
    population, but the package does not yet expose this scenario.
11. **Calibration helpers for severity ranges:** small helpers that
    read validation-literature parameters (PPV, sensitivity, claims-
    accuracy ranges) from a YAML file and translate them into
    `data_quality_scenarios` lists, with the citations attached to
    the audit log.

## When to use cleanTMLE inside a broader governance arrangement

For exploratory or lower-stakes RWE studies, cleanTMLE used on
its own may be adequate to document and audit outcome-blind
estimator selection: the analyst prespecifies the analytic plan,
runs the workflow inside a single R session, and archives the
analysis lock together with the audit and decision logs. For
high-stakes regulatory or confirmatory studies (FDA, EMA, or HTA
submission contexts), cleanTMLE should be embedded within
personnel-based outcome-blinding and access-control arrangements.
That deployment places cleanTMLE inside a broader governed
process with separate study-level work items: source-data audit
and provenance, exposure and outcome phenotype validation,
role-separated analyst and reviewer access, and an independent
review of the pre-outcome decision by personnel who did not
author the analytic plan. The software-mediated workflow records
that the prespecified contract has been followed; the governed
process establishes that the contract is the right one
[@muntner2024staging; @fda2018rwe; @ema2024guide].

## Recommendations for practice

A fillable SAP template aligned with the prespecification checklist
of @gruber2022sap and the staging construct of @muntner2024staging
is shipped with the package as
`system.file("templates", "sap_template.qmd", package = "cleanTMLE")`.
The template walks the analyst through the eight-section structure
(estimand under ICH E9(R1), identifiability assumptions and DQ
mappings, candidate grid, decision thresholds, NC domain coverage,
sensitivity plan, decision log, reporting checklist) so that the
prespecification is filed in the same form that the audit log will
later reference.

We recommend a five-step pre-outcome workflow when the analyst is
preparing a TL-RWE study.

1. Document the SPIFD2 template, citing validation studies or data
   profiling for each plausible range.
2. Lock the specification and declare the estimand ladder: the
   primary estimand, the ordered fallbacks, the switching trigger,
   and the decision thresholds, all before any simulation runs.
3. Fit the propensity and read the design: `assess_support()`,
   `estimand_feasibility()`, and `simulate_support()`. If the
   declared primary is unsupported, the ladder, not the analyst's
   discretion, chooses what replaces it.
4. Run `run_plasmode_feasibility()` and `run_plasmode_dq_stress()`
   on the surviving estimand. Use the SPIFD2-derived ranges as the
   inputs to `data_quality_scenarios`.
5. Assemble `design_report()` and score the pre-outcome decision. If
   a candidate is robust to the SPIFD2 plausible ranges, lock it. If
   no candidate is robust, the correct decision is to stop, and the
   analyst should reconsider the data source, the estimand, or the
   decision thresholds before unblinding.

The design log preserves all of the above. The final paper or
regulatory submission can be reconstructed from the lock and the
log, including the SPIFD2 ranges, the support and feasibility
verdicts, the plasmode and DQ stress metrics, the pre-outcome
decision, and the post-outcome estimates with any ladder switch.

# Summary {#sec-summary}

cleanTMLE is an R package for staged, outcome-blind targeted learning
that makes estimability a design-stage question and produces
reproducible prespecification records. A traditional clean room
establishes that the analyst did not peek; cleanTMLE additionally
establishes whether the promised comparison was answerable, names the
neighbouring estimand the data can support when it is not, and
estimates that estimand with a doubly robust estimator, all committed
before anyone saw an outcome. The support assessment, the
per-estimand feasibility reading, the outcome-blind support map
(built on the generate-treatment plasmode design of
@shaw2025plasmode), and the pre-registered estimand ladder implement
the estimability half. The data-quality stress test implements the
robustness half: it extends the outcome-blind plasmode loop of
@dang2023roadmap and @gruber2022sap with five data-quality
degradation mechanisms, producing per-candidate degradation gradients
on the same bias, RMSE, and coverage scale as the baseline plasmode
so the prespecified decision rule applies uniformly to both, and a
constructed demonstration (@sec-divergence) shows the worst-case rule
can lock a different candidate from the baseline rule. The package
does not itself determine whether a data source is fit for purpose;
the severity ranges entered into the stress test must come from prior
validation studies, data profiling, or expert elicitation, and the
support machinery reads only the measured covariates. The
analysis-lock object and design log persist the prespecification as
reproducible records. The package is available at
<https://github.com/amertens/cleanTMLE>;
the simulation code for the results in @sec-simulation is in
the companion repository <https://github.com/amertens/clean-room-sim>.

# Reproducibility {#sec-reproducibility}

The cleanTMLE package ships 22 testthat test files covering the core
workflow: analysis-lock creation and validation, the support assessment
and per-estimand feasibility functions, the estimand ladder and its
estimators (including recovery of known ATT and ATO truths and the
Shaw-artifact design comparison), the DQ stress-test mechanics and
degradation gradients, bootstrap and influence-function variance
estimators (including the `"match_tmle"` estimator), event-process
helpers, plasmode simulation, estimator ground-truth comparisons
against `tmle::tmle()`, and reporting tables. Tests are run on every
push via the repository's continuous-integration configuration
(`cleanTMLE/tests/testthat/`). The experimental time-to-event
estimators have separate test files and are tagged accordingly.

## Estimator validation against a reference implementation {#sec-validation}

Beyond the unit tests, we validate the package's targeted-learning estimator
against the reference `tmle` package on a single large sample ($n = 20{,}000$)
from the Scenario A data-generating process, where the analytic marginal risk
difference is known. The results show the cleanTMLE TMLE and `tmle::tmle()`
agreeing to roughly four decimal places (a difference near $0.0002$ in the
risk difference, with
near-identical standard errors), and both recovering the analytic truth
(@tbl-validation). This establishes that the estimator machinery is a correct
implementation; the package's distinct contributions are the staged
outcome-blind governance and the data-quality stress test layered on top of a
standard, validated estimator.

```{r eval = file.exists("../sandbox/validation/validation_vs_tmle.csv")}
#| label: tbl-validation
#| tbl-cap: "cleanTMLE TMLE versus the reference tmle package and the analytic truth on identical data (Scenario A DGP, n = 20,000). diff_vs_tmle is the cleanTMLE estimate minus the tmle::tmle estimate."
v <- read.csv("../sandbox/validation/validation_vs_tmle.csv", check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(v)
```

The simulation results reported in this paper are produced by the
scripts listed below in the companion repository
(<https://github.com/amertens/clean-room-sim>). Each writes to a
tracked results directory: `results_new/` for the main simulation and
the variance study, `rescueCo/results/` for the case study, and
`sandbox/` for the divergence and validation studies. Replicate counts,
sample size, and output directory for the main simulation are set with
the `SIM_REPS`, `SIM_NOBS`, and `SIM_RESULTS` environment variables (see
`RUN_MANIFEST.md`).

| Script | Output file(s) | Figures / tables |
|---|---|---|
| `run_simulation.R` | `results_new/simulation_results.rds`, `results_new/summary_*.csv` | per-scenario metrics tables in @sec-simulation, @fig-mc-boxplots, @fig-coverage-bar, @fig-se-calibration, @fig-mc-forest, @fig-dq-degradation |
| `run_gate_operating_characteristics.R` | `results_new/gate_oc.rds` | @tbl-gate-oc, @sec-gate-oc |
| `_bootstrap_variance.R` | `results_new/bootstrap_variance.rds`, `results_new/bootstrap_variance.csv` | @tbl-boot-variance |
| `sandbox/validation/validate_vs_tmle.R` | `sandbox/validation/validation_vs_tmle.csv` | @tbl-validation |
| `rescueCo/scripts/10_multiarm_build.R` | `rescueCo/results/multiarm/multiarm_locks.rds`, `lock_summary.csv` | Case-study locks (@tbl-cs-locks) |
| `rescueCo/scripts/11_multiarm_design.R`, `11b_nc_ladder_unadjusted.R` | `support_by_contrast.csv`, `estimand_feasibility.csv`, `who_is_unsupported.csv`, `violation_regions.csv`, `nc_ladder.csv`, `collider_check.csv`, support figures | @sec-casestudy-support tables and figures |
| `rescueCo/scripts/12_multiarm_support_sim.R` | `supportsim_*.rds`, `designcmp_*.rds`, support-map figures | Support maps and @tbl-cs-designcmp |
| `rescueCo/scripts/13_multiarm_estimation.R`, `14_multiarm_report.R` | `ladder_estimates.csv`, `ladder_design_log.csv` | @tbl-cs-ladder |
| `rescueCo/scripts/build_reconciliation_table.R` | `rescueCo/results/reconciliation_table.csv` | Reconciliation against the parallel unblinded analysis |
| `rescueCo/scripts/rescueco_dq_full.R` | `rescueCo/results/plasmode_dq_stress.rds`, `rescueCo/results/plasmode_dq_degradation.csv` | Case-study DQ subsection (@sec-casestudy-dq) |
| `sandbox/rescueco_fidelity/plasmode_fidelity.R` | `rescueCo/results/plasmode_fidelity.csv` | Case-study synthetic-outcome fidelity subsection |
| `sandbox/candidate_divergence/divergence_study.R` | `candidate_divergence_full.rds`, `degradation_gradient.png` | @sec-divergence (@fig-divergence) |

: Script-to-output map. Running the scripts in order fully
regenerates the tracked simulation outputs; rendering the `.qmd` then
produces all figures and tables. The underscore-prefixed scripts
(`dev/`) are diagnostic utilities not required for manuscript
reproduction.

The case-study DQ results reported in @sec-casestudy-dq use a
50-replicate illustrative run produced by
`rescueCo/scripts/rescueco_dq_full.R` (a 200-replicate confirmation is
deferred, as the case study is a workflow demonstration rather than
confirmatory evidence). The
bundled configuration (`config/clean_room_config.yml`) runs Stage 2c
at 3 replicates per threat-severity cell as a continuous-integration
smoke test, which is not used for any reported result.

# Appendix {#sec-appendix .unnumbered}

## Conceptual layers of the workflow

@tbl-layers distinguishes the conceptual layers that the workflow keeps
separate, and is a reference for which decisions are addressed at
the design stage versus the estimation stage.

```{r layers-table}
#| label: tbl-layers
layers <- data.frame(
  Layer = c(
    "Causal question",
    "Causal estimand",
    "Identification assumptions",
    "Statistical estimand",
    "Estimand ladder",
    "Estimator",
    "Pre-outcome diagnostic metric",
    "Governance decision"),
  Description = c(
    "Clinical or policy question framed as a target trial or causal contrast.",
    "Counterfactual treatment effect of interest (e.g. marginal risk difference).",
    "Conditions under which the causal estimand can be expressed as an observed-data parameter (exchangeability, positivity, consistency, measurement validity, missingness assumptions).",
    "Observed-data parameter identified under the assumptions above.",
    "Pre-registered ordered fallbacks (trimmed ATE, ATT, ATO) and the support verdict that triggers a switch when the declared primary is not estimable in practice.",
    "Algorithm used to estimate the statistical estimand, for example TMLE, IPTW, or matching.",
    "Pre-outcome quantity used for design checks: support verdict, per-estimand feasibility, simulated bias, RMSE, coverage, effective sample size, balance, negative-control performance.",
    "Whether prespecified criteria support proceeding, require additional review, or require stopping the analysis before the outcome is examined."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(layers,
             caption = "Conceptual layers in the staged workflow. The same vocabulary is used throughout the manuscript to keep estimand, estimator, simulation, and decision rule distinct.")
```

## The package inside the causal roadmap

@fig-roadmap shows where the package sits in the roadmap, and
@fig-governance shows the software arrangement as one layer of a broader
governance stack in which external validation, independent oversight,
and data standards remain necessary inputs to the pre-outcome decision.

![cleanTMLE inside the causal roadmap. Boxes shaded grey indicate work that the package can operationalise; the remaining boxes are external study-level activities.](figures/fig-roadmap.png){#fig-roadmap width=70%}

![Governance layers. The software-level arrangement is necessary but not sufficient for regulatory or confirmatory RWE; external validation, independent review, and data standards feed the pre-outcome decision.](figures/fig-governance.png){#fig-governance width=90%}

## Regulatory alignment

@tbl-reg-align maps each roadmap component to the corresponding
manuscript section, the relevant FDA, EMA, and ICH expectation, what
cleanTMLE can operationalise in software, and what still requires
external study-level justification. The final column is the one that
distinguishes the software-level workflow from the broader regulatory
governance arrangement.

## Event-process and diagnostic helpers

@tbl-event-diag lists the additional event-process and diagnostic
structures the workflow makes explicit.

```{r event-diag-table}
#| label: tbl-event-diag
event_diag <- data.frame(
  Component = c(
    "Event-process classification",
    "Target population and reference group",
    "Treatment, censoring, and missingness weight diagnostics",
    "Competing-risk and composite-risk coherence check",
    "Cumulative-risk reporting table",
    "Hazard-ratio de-emphasis"),
  Purpose = c(
    "Map each post-baseline event to its role in the estimand and ICH E9(R1) intercurrent-event strategy.",
    "Force explicit declaration of the population and reference group for every contrast.",
    "Report percentiles, ESS, extreme-weight counts, and weighted SMDs for each weight vector used.",
    "Verify that event-of-interest plus competing-event cumulative incidences are coherent with the composite risk.",
    "Single structured table of cumulative risks, contrasts, event counts, and estimator name.",
    "Cumulative risks, risk differences, and risk ratios are the primary summaries; hazard ratios are reported only as secondary when the estimand is explicitly hazard-based."),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(event_diag,
             caption = "Supplementary mapping. Event-process and diagnostic structures that the workflow makes explicit.")
```
